name: Patong Beach
label: Patong Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Patong Beach Viewpoint' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Clean Patong beach' (node/10692792305): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Phuket's busiest beach and nightlife hub.

text.description:
Patong is the busiest beach resort on Phuket's west coast, and its long, curving beach runs the whole length of the town's western side, roughly 2.85 km (1.77 miles) end to end. It became popular with Western visitors in the late 1980s and has grown into the island's main tourist resort, with many hotels and the centre of its shopping and nightlife. The town was hit hard by the tsunami of 26 December 2004, but it has largely recovered.

The best phone view is from above rather than from the sand. That height lets you fit the whole sweep of the bay into one frame, which is hard to do at ground level. Sunset is the moment to aim for, when the scene warms up and the lights start to come on along the front.

There is also a lot to see once you walk down to the beach. Umbrellas, sunbathers and boats make good small scenes, and the evening crowds add life to your shots. If you want a second angle, the hillside viewpoints at Wat Doi Thepnimit and Kalim both look back over Patong Bay. Kalim is quieter and reached by road.
text.geographic_location: Patong is on the west coast of Phuket, in the island's main tourist resort area. The beach runs along the western edge of the town. The Patong Beach Viewpoint is listed on Thawewong Road, a hillside road above the beach, so check the exact spot on the map.
text.directions_text: No railway station or tram stop is listed near this spot. From there, Patong Beach is about 960 m to the south (roughly 15 minutes on foot). The Patong Beach Viewpoint is listed on Thawewong Road, so check the exact spot on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the bay, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details on the beach below, such as umbrellas, boats or people on the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Patong Beach Viewpoint (on Thawewong Road, the road that runs along the hill above the beach). An elevated panorama where the town meets the sea, with the beach and its activity visible below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line where the sand meets the sea along the lower third, leaving the sky and the water as the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. Try a slow panorama to sweep along the bay, or zoom in for a closer shot of one busy patch of beach. For a different angle, the viewpoints at Wat Doi Thepnimit and Kalim also overlook the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours don't wash out. After the sun has gone, switch to night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the lights sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the light warms up and the lights below start to come on. Go a little early to find a good spot.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is listed as free; check local signs before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Patong Beach faces west towards the Andaman Sea, so the sun sets over the water.
The viewpoint may be busier around sunset.
Resting your elbows on a wall or railing helps keep night shots steady, if a safe railing or wall is available.
From the stand-here point, Patong Beach is about 960 m to the south, roughly 15 minutes on foot (an estimate: 962 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).

name: Phuket Old Town
label: Phuket Old Town
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Phuket Old Town'.
notes: Sino-Portuguese shophouses and colourful streets in the heart of Phuket Town.

text.description:
Phuket Old Town is the historic part of Phuket Town, and it photographs well because the streets are lined on both sides with Sino-Portuguese buildings. The main streets are Thalang, Phang Nga, Krabi, Dibuk and Yoawarat. Many of the old shophouses and mansions have become shops, hotels, restaurants and museums, so there is usually something to frame in the foreground, such as a doorway, a sign or a café table.

The area grew rich on tin mining. Hokkien Chinese miners did much of the work in the 18th century and helped build the old part of the city. In the early 20th century, roads and canals were built and European mining companies were invited in. Many buildings from that time have been preserved and restored. The area is also tied to the Baba community, which came from early unions between Hokkien tin-miners and Siamese women.

For your phone, think in rows and repeats. Repeating shopfronts and arches make good leading lines down a street. Close detail shots, such as window shutters, tiled floors and door carvings, work as well as wide views. Walk slowly and look up, because the upper floors are often the most interesting part. Stand at a corner to catch two streets in one frame, and keep an eye on traffic when you step back to compose.
text.geographic_location: Phuket Old Town is an area of historical interest in the city of Phuket. Its main streets are Thalang, Phang Nga, Krabi, Dibuk and Yoawarat.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby, so start from Phuket Town and walk to the phone icon on the map. Walk west for about 6 minutes on foot to reach its streets. The phone icon on the map is about 370 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for whole street scenes, then switch to the default lens (1x) for shopfronts. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for upper-floor details and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take your main photos there, on the pavement at a street corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the rows of shophouses so the verticals stay straight. Use the street as a leading line towards a distant corner. Keep a doorway or signboard in the foreground for depth. Then take a few close-ups of decorative details with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so bright walls keep their colour. Use portrait mode if you photograph a person in front of a shopfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the streets are likely to be quieter and the light softer.

text.access_note: The streets are open public space, but individual museums, shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go to any of them.

name: Kata Beach
label: Kata Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kata Noi Viewpoint' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The Peaks Residence Kata noi' (pois).
notes: Popular sandy beach with clear water.

text.description: Kata Beach is a 1.5-kilometre stretch of sand on Phuket's west coast, facing the Andaman Sea. It is split into two halves: Kata Yai in the north and Kata Noi in the south. Hotels and restaurants sit close to the sand, so it is a busy, lively place at ground level. For a calmer picture, look at the beach from above. The Kata Noi Viewpoint is a small roadside lookout on the road between Kata and Nai Harn. From here you look down onto Kata Noi and its turquoise bay, and on a clear day the Big Buddha may show on the distant hill. It is a more intimate, compact view than the busier Karon viewpoint, and it works well at sunset. Some of the best spots on the terrace belong to the café there and are for customers, but the view from the roadside is free. Access to the Big Buddha itself has been closed since a landslide in August 2024, so this distant glimpse may be the nearest you get. If you want all three bays (Kata Noi, Kata and Karon) in one wide frame, with the little island of Koh Pu just off Kata, the Karon Viewpoint is the alternative, though it gets very crowded at sunset. Take care at the roadside: stay off the carriageway and watch for passing scooters.
text.geographic_location: Kata Beach is on the west coast of Phuket, about 17 kilometres from Phuket Town, and is relatively close to Karon Beach and Patong Beach. The Kata Noi Viewpoint sits on the hill road between Kata and Nai Harn.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve this part of Phuket, so go by taxi or hired scooter from Kata and ask for the Kata Noi Viewpoint on the road towards Nai Harn. The viewpoint is on the hill above the bay, with Kata Beach itself to the north. The beach position on the map is about 1.5 km to the north of the viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the bay and the sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier crop of the water and sand. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the Big Buddha on the far hill, when it is visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kata Noi Viewpoint (small roadside lookout above the bay, on the road between Kata and Nai Harn). A close, compact view down onto Kata Noi Beach and its turquoise bay, with the Big Buddha sometimes visible on the hill in the distance. From here you look down onto Kata Noi Beach and its turquoise water, and the main part of Kata Beach lies further to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, keeping it level. Include a little of the curve of the shore to lead the eye into the bay. For all three bays in one wide frame, try the Karon Viewpoint instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch at sunset to keep the colours rich and stop the sky turning white. Try Night mode only once the light has nearly gone, and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the cove is most atmospheric. Arrive a little early to get a spot at the roadside.

text.access_note: The roadside view is free and open to the public, but the best terrace spots are reserved for café customers.
claims_not_in_sources: The sun sets over the sea to the west, so the bay faces the sunset.
The roadside lookout is small, so space may be limited at busy times.
Scooters pass along the road by the viewpoint.

name: Karon Beach
label: Karon Beach
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Long stretch of white sand on the west coast.

text.description: Karon Beach is a long stretch of sand on Phuket's west coast, with a town of the same name running alongside it. It is the second longest beach in the province, which is the main reason it works so well on a phone: there is plenty of room to step back and fit the whole sweep of the shore into one frame. It is generally quieter than neighbouring Patong and is popular with families and couples. That mix of people gives you easy, relaxed scenes: paddlers at the water's edge, a couple strolling, children playing in the shallows. It also has a loyal following among Scandinavian visitors, and many local businesses cater to them. The beach was badly damaged by the tsunamis that followed the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake, especially in the south, but it had largely recovered by 2008. Keep the horizon level and let the curve of the shore lead the eye through the picture. Then move in for smaller scenes: footprints, a line of waves, people at a distance. If you want people in your shot, a little patience helps. Wait for a walker to reach a gap in the frame rather than chasing them. Wipe your lens first, as sea air and sunscreen smear it quickly.
text.geographic_location: On the west coast of Phuket, where the town of Karon sits right behind its long beach. It is generally quieter than neighbouring Patong.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the town of Karon by whatever local transport suits you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of sand and sea. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking scenes with people, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details at a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Karon Viewpoint (hilltop platform, facing north over the bays). A panorama of Kata Noi, Kata and Karon beaches in one frame, with the sea and Koh Pu island beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon or the waterline on a line so the shot looks level. Include a strip of wet sand or a curve of shoreline in the foreground to give depth. For a longer view along the beach, try panorama mode and sweep slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or sand to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or bright sand looks washed out. Wipe the lens before shooting, because salty air leaves a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on a west-facing coast, and the beach is often calmer early in the morning. Midday sun is harsh and flattens the colours.

text.access_note: Check locally for access details before you go.

name: Big Buddha
label: Big Buddha
camera_pill: near ซอยยอดเสน่ห์ 1
pin_note: Position from OSM W242673270 (Phuket Big Buddha): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: 45 m white marble Buddha on the Nakkerd Hills with island views.

text.description:
The Big Buddha is a large seated Buddha statue on Phuket island, ranked 5th among the photo spots on the Phuket map. The open view around it makes it a simple, clear subject for a phone, and it is a good place for a wide photo of the whole figure with the sky above it.

You will be looking up at it from a short distance, so the figure will not fit in the default lens (1x) unless you step back. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole statue in with plenty of sky, and keep the phone level so the sides do not lean inwards too much. Then switch to the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the face or the folded hands, which will look flatter and calmer than a wide shot.

A statue against a bright sky can fool the exposure. Tap the statue to focus and slide the exposure down a little if it looks washed out. Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon and the statue's base straight. Visitors may be walking through your frame, so wait a moment for a clearer view or include people to give a sense of scale. Please take photos quietly and respectfully, and check local signs for any visiting rules.
text.geographic_location: The Big Buddha is on Phuket island.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed near this spot, so check a local map for how to get there. Walk towards the north-east and the statue will be in front of you. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole statue and the sky in from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view once you have stepped back. Use the telephoto (2x-5x) for the face and hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. If the figure does not fit in the frame, take a few steps back rather than tilting the phone upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and level and use the gridlines to keep the base of the statue straight. Leave some sky above the head. For a second picture, zoom in on the face or hands and fill the frame with them. Try one photo with a few visitors in it to show how big the statue is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright areas do not wash out. If your phone has it, try a Live Photo to catch the moment when people move out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a bluer sky. Midday sun can be harsh and wash out detail.

text.access_note: Check local signs for any visiting rules.

name: Wat Chalong
label: Wat Chalong
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Chalong' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wat Chalong' (way/242673271): middle (460 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/242673271: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Chalong' (461 m across).
notes: Phuket's most important Buddhist temple with ornate pagoda.

text.description:
Wat Chalong is the most important of Phuket's 29 Buddhist temples, and it is a lively, colourful place to point a phone. Its official name is Wat Chaiyathararam. It is dedicated to two respected monks, Luang Pho Chaem and Luang Pho Chuang, who led the people of Chalong against the Chinese rebellion in 1876 and used their knowledge of herbal medicine to help the injured. That story is a nice thing to know as you walk around.

The ordination hall (the ubosot) is the subject. Look for its layered roof, with its ornate tassels and serpent decorations, against the sky. The red-and-gold exterior is what makes the shot work. The colours are strong, and the stacked roof lines give you a pattern to build the picture around.

The grounds are busy. A market spills into the temple area, and tour coaches tend to arrive from mid-morning into the early afternoon, so go early if you want clean frames. The tall gilded pagoda is a good second picture, and the calmer corners with greenery and water in the foreground make a quieter third.

This is a working temple. Ask before photographing worshippers or monks, keep the flash off, and do not photograph inside the prayer halls during ceremonies. Photography of the relic chamber is restricted.
text.geographic_location: Wat Chalong is in the Chalong Subdistrict of Mueang Phuket District, Phuket. The temple grounds are large, and a market runs into them.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed near Wat Chalong, so plan your own way there and ask for Wat Chalong, also known as Wat Chaiyathararam. Once inside the grounds, head for the middle of the temple grounds. The ordination hall is the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole ordination hall. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof tassels and serpent decorations. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the full height of the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Wat Chalong (exterior of the ordination hall (ubosot), framing the roofline against the sky). The layered roof with its ornate tassels and serpent decorations, set against blue sky. Face west, towards the middle of the temple grounds, and look for the ordination hall's roofline, which should frame against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone up slightly so the roof layers fill the upper part of the frame, and turn on gridlines to keep the roof edges straight. Leave some blue sky above as a clean backdrop. For a different shot, try the gilded pagoda rising against the sky, or the pagoda and buildings framed by greenery and water in a calmer part of the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sky or the gold trim to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the red and gold keep their colour. Keep the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day, before the tour coaches arrive from mid-morning, for fewer people in your frame and softer light.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress respectfully and follow local rules on photography; check the official site before you go.

name: Promthep Cape
label: Promthep Cape
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'แหลมพรหมเทพ' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'แหลมพรหมเทพ' (node/265689795): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM N5318388527 (Promthep Cape Monastery): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Southern headland famous for sunsets and lighthouse.

text.description:
Promthep Cape (Laem Phromthep in Thai) is a rocky headland on Phuket, and it is one of the island's best-known places to watch the sun go down. From the cliff-edge main platform you look west over the Andaman Sea. The rocky point and its palm-lined edge sit in the foreground, with islands out on the horizon. When the sunset lights it, you get the classic postcard picture that most visitors come for.

The cape is very popular, and in peak season it gets crowded. The car park can be full by about 17:30, and some guides suggest arriving 45 to 90 minutes before sunset. That gives you time to find a good spot on the platform and try a few frames while the light is still soft. Arriving early also lets you look around for a clearer view.

If you have time, there are two other good pictures nearby. The white Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse looks good against the evening sky and sea. You can photograph it from outside, but lighthouse entry is restricted, so check locally if you want to go inside. The Windmill Viewpoint is the other option. It shows Ya Nui Beach in the foreground with the cape far off across the bay, so the cape will look small there.

On your phone, keep the shots simple. Choose your view early, then wait for the sky to warm up.
text.geographic_location: Promthep Cape is a headland on Phuket, close to Ya Nui Beach. It is where the land meets the Andaman Sea.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so there is no station to use as a start point. The cape is reached by road to the car park. Park there and walk to the main platform on the cliff edge. Parking arrangements can vary and lighthouse entry is restricted, so check locally before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the headland, the palms and the sea together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the platform is busy and you want the whole sweep of coast and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the islands on the horizon or to bring the lighthouse closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (cliff-edge main platform, facing west toward the sea). The cape's rocky headland and palm-lined edge with the Andaman Sea and offshore islands behind, lit by the sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line rather than in the middle. Let the rocks and palms fill the foreground and leave the rest to the sky and sea. If you have time, take a second photo of the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse against the evening sky. Alternatively, the Windmill Viewpoint shows Ya Nui Beach with the cape far off across the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. Take a few frames as the light changes. Live Photos can help you pick the best moment if people move in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset. Check the sunset time for your date, because it changes through the year. In peak season, plan to arrive 45 to 90 minutes beforehand to get a parking space and a good spot on the platform.

text.access_note: This is a popular public viewpoint; parking arrangements can vary and lighthouse entry is restricted, so check locally before you go.

name: Phuket FantaSea
label: Phuket FantaSea
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2089159: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Themed cultural park and evening show.

text.description:
Phuket FantaSea is a Thai cultural theme park that comes alive after dark. It covers about 60 acres (20 ha) and opened to the public on 20 December 1998. The park includes a theatre show, a very large buffet restaurant and a shopping street called Festival Village. The show is staged in the 'Palace of the Elephants', a purpose-built theatre that reproduces a Sukhothai-era stone elephant palace. It has three floors and seats 3,000. The Golden Kinnaree buffet restaurant is built in an Ayutthaya-era style and can seat 4,000 guests.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the architecture and the evening atmosphere. The big temple-style buildings and carved details make strong subjects, and the shopping street gives you lively scenes with people and lights. Start with a wide shot to show the scale of a building, then move closer for details such as carvings and decoration. Look for a clear line to the building and keep passers-by at the edges of the frame if you want a calmer picture. Rules on photography inside the theatre and in some areas of the park may differ from the open areas, so check the official site before you go and follow staff instructions on the day.
text.geographic_location: Phuket FantaSea is on the island of Phuket, in the south of Thailand.
text.directions_text: The nearest stations or stops are not listed for this spot. Use a map app to reach Phuket FantaSea on Phuket island. Once you are inside the park grounds, the phone icon on the map is where the photo is taken, so you do not need to walk any further. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit a whole building into the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for most shots, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carvings, roof details and decorations.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is right there with you, so you are looking at the buildings and the lit-up surroundings rather than a distant view. If the area is busy, take a few steps to one side to get a clearer line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight so it does not look as if it is leaning. Try one wide shot, then one closer shot of a detail. People walking through the foreground can add scale and life to a wide picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, let night mode do its work and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing for the second or two it needs. Tap on a bright part of the building to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so the lights do not blow out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the evening, because this is a nighttime park. Aim for dusk, when the sky still has some colour and the lights are on.

text.access_note: Phuket FantaSea is a theme park. Check the official site before you go for current opening and entry details.

name: Nai Harn Beach
label: Nai Harn Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Windmill Viewpoint' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Windmill Viewpoint' (node/2513821648): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM R6162518 (Nai Harn Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Quiet bay with lagoon and mountain backdrop.

text.description:
Nai Harn Beach is a crescent of sand on Phuket's Andaman coast, and the best way to photograph it is from above. The Windmill Viewpoint sits on the hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches. From there the whole bay curves out below you, with Ya Nui Beach and Promthep Cape in the distance. The white wind turbines on the hill sit in the frame and give the scene a bit of character. It is quieter than Promthep Cape and, as far as we know, free to visit.

The sweep of the bay and the layers of sea, sand and headland suit a phone well. Open the camera, turn on the gridlines and put the curve of the beach along a lower third line, leaving the rest for sea and sky. A turbine at one edge adds a sense of scale. If you want the beach as a smaller part of a bigger seascape, Black Rock Viewpoint also looks down over the bay and the open sea, though its access road is described as hard to find, so check the route first. For ground-level shots, the beach itself has granite boulders that work as a foreground, with the green hill behind.

Late afternoon to sunset is the usual recommendation. One guide suggests early morning if you want the clearest, stillest water. The monsoon season runs from May to October.
text.geographic_location: Nai Harn Beach is on Phuket's Andaman coast. The Windmill Viewpoint is on the hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches, reached from Wiset Road.
text.directions_text: Head for Nai Harn and Wiset Road, then follow the road up to the hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches. No station or tram stop serves this area, but the hilltop is walkable or easy by scooter. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole bay and the turbines in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Promthep Cape or Ya Nui Beach in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Windmill Viewpoint (hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches, facing the Andaman Sea). A high, wide view down over Nai Harn Bay and its crescent of sand, with Ya Nui Beach and Promthep Cape in the distance and the white wind turbines in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the curve of the beach along the lower third, so sea and sky fill the rest. Keep a turbine at one side for scale. If you have time, Black Rock Viewpoint gives a wider panorama where the beach is a smaller part of the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or sand to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour near sunset. Panorama mode suits the long curve of the bay, so move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset. For the clearest, stillest water, try early morning. Note the monsoon season runs May to October.

text.access_note: The Windmill Viewpoint is described as a free, open hilltop viewpoint, but check locally before you go, as current access could not be confirmed.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light and sunset colour suit this west-facing coast.
A telephoto lens can pull Promthep Cape and Ya Nui Beach closer in the frame.

notes: Hilltop lookout over Nai Harn and Yanui beaches.

text.description:
Windmill Viewpoint is a small hilltop on Wisit Road, between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches, in the far south of Phuket. A cluster of tall white wind turbines stands on the top, part of the Promthep Alternative Energy Station, and the ground drops away to the Andaman Sea on the other side. That mix of sea, sky and simple white shapes is why it works so well on a phone.

There are two good pictures here. The first is the classic one: the turbines close by in the foreground, with the blades framed by water and sky. The second is calmer and often better. Walk to the edge of the flat, wide top, away from the turbine cluster, and face south. From there you get open sea and the headland of Promthep Cape, with its access path visible, and the cliff edge gives a clear line out to it. The top is wide enough to find some space even when other visitors are about.

The small car park fills up at sunset, so if you want a quiet spot to yourself, arrive earlier. The road up is steep and winding, and tuk-tuks can slow the traffic, so allow a little extra time. Keep back from the cliff edge when you compose a shot, and take care in wind when you hold your phone out over the view.
text.geographic_location: On a small hilltop on Wisit Road in southern Phuket, between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches, looking towards Promthep Cape.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or similar stop nearby that we can give you. Start from the Nai Harn or Ya Nui beach area in the far south of Phuket and follow Wisit Road up to the hilltop. The road is steep and winding, so take it slowly. Once you park, the phone icon on the map is right on the hilltop, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of sea and headland, or the turbines with sky above. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of Promthep Cape. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pull the headland and its path closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see open sea and the headland with its access path, well away from the turbine cluster.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with the headland sitting off-centre. For the alternative shot, walk towards the turbines and use one tall turbine in the foreground, with the blades set against water and sky. Keep your phone level so the horizon stays straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the headland to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Around sunset, check the screen before you shoot, as the bright sky can darken the foreground. A short panorama along the cliff edge also works well, if you hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset gives the most atmosphere, but the car park fills then, so arrive early. Earlier in the day it is quieter and easier to find space on the plateau.

text.access_note: Open public hilltop, free to visit and open at all hours; the small car park fills at sunset, and it is still worth checking locally before you go.

label: Khao Rang Viewpoint
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Khao Rang Viewpoint' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Hill with a panoramic view of Phuket Town.

text.description: Khao Rang is the hill above Phuket Town, and its summit gives a bird's-eye view over the town and out towards the coast. The hill is not high, but the top still shows the old-town grid of streets and rooftops. Up on the summit there is a terrace and a landscaped garden, and a white pavilion with a dome. That pavilion is the main thing to photograph. It works well as a foreground element, so you can stand with it in the corner of the frame and let the town fill the background. The view is the subject here rather than the hill itself, so you take your photos from the top, not of it. The summit is free to enter and open all day. It can be busy around sunset, and monkeys roam the car park and grounds, so keep food out of sight and don't hold your phone loosely near them. The white structure has reportedly been partly covered during renovations, so check its current state before you go. A listing also names a pavilion-style lookout as a possible extra viewpoint, but its location is unconfirmed, so check it on the map before relying on it.
text.geographic_location: Khao Rang is a hill above Phuket Town. Its summit looks down over the old town and towards the coast.
text.directions_text: Start from Phuket Town and follow the map to the phone icon on the map at the summit of Khao Rang Viewpoint. The terrace and garden are at the top. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view over the town with the white pavilion in the corner. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole dome, garden and sky in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out parts of the old-town grid and the coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is at this same spot, so you are photographing from the hilltop itself. From here you look out over Phuket Town's old-town grid and the coastline, with the white pavilion dome beside you as a foreground element.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pavilion on one side so the town fills the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level and include some of the garden or terrace edge in the foreground for depth. A listing also names a pavilion-style lookout; check its location on the map first before treating it as an alternative viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the town to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode for the city lights and rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady. Keep your phone secure if monkeys are around.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: 17:00–18:30 for sunset and the city lights, though it can be crowded then. 07:00–09:00 is quieter.

text.access_note: The summit viewpoint is a free public space open all day, but check the current state of the white pavilion before you go, as it may be under renovation.

label: Thai Hua Museum

notes: Neoclassical former Chinese school building in Old Town.

text.description:
Phuket Thai Hua Museum sits in a 1934 mansion in Phuket Old Town, and its front is the reason to stop with a phone in hand. The two-storey Sino-Portuguese facade has an arched entrance, shuttered windows and decorative plasterwork, and together they make a tidy, colourful composition that suits a straight-on shot. The museum is on Krabi Road, a quiet side street just east of Thalang Road, so it is easy to pair with a stroll through the old town.

The front facade is the main photo point. The outside of the building can be photographed from the street without going in, which makes it an easy quick stop. Interior photography may need a separate pass, so check opening days before you go if you plan to shoot inside.

For a first picture, stand in front of the entrance and centre the arch, using the gridlines to keep the shutters and walls upright. Then move in for a close shot of the plasterwork around the windows and doorway. For something calmer than the busy front, look for the quieter, older-looking corner at the back of the museum, where old roof tiles are stacked. It gives a more weathered, textured picture and makes a good second frame. Morning or late afternoon is the time one guide suggests for exterior photos.
text.geographic_location: In Phuket Old Town, on Krabi Road, a quiet side street just east of Thalang Road.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops near here, so start from Thalang Road in Phuket Old Town and head east onto Krabi Road. Navigate to Krabi Road, just east of Thalang Road. The museum is on the street itself, so you can photograph the front as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit both storeys, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the plasterwork and shutters.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back onto the street in front of พิพิธภัณฑ์ภูเก็ตไทยหัว, facing the front facade on Krabi Road, so you can fit the whole front in. From there you see the whole Sino-Portuguese front with its arched entrance and shuttered windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the arch and turn on the gridlines so the walls and shutters stay straight. Hold the phone level and keep it at chest height to limit leaning verticals. Then zoom in on the plasterwork for a detail shot. For a different picture, try the quieter back corner of the museum with the stacked old roof tiles in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out, or up if the shaded front looks dark. Wipe the lens first, as street dust can soften the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, according to one guide, for exterior photos.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but interior photography and opening days may vary, so check opening days before you go.

label: Kamala Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Laem Singh Viewpoint' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Laem Singh viewpoint' (node/3983421103): point.

text.description: Kamala Beach is a long curve of sand on Phuket's west side, with the open Andaman Sea in front of it. It photographs best from a little way off, where you can see the whole curve at once. The roadside lookout at Laem Singh, on the headland between Kamala and Surin, is the classic place for this. From there the beach sweeps away below a palm-fringed headland, with the sea beyond. It is described as a favourite spot for wide sunset shots, and it costs nothing to stop there. Trees can block the sunset from the lookout itself, so look at the sky and the trees before you settle in. Walkers can reach it from the north end of Kamala Beach along the coastal road. If you want other angles, Kamala Viewpoint is said to show the whole length of the beach in one frame, so check it on the day. Wat Baan Kamala is another option, with its garden, bell tower and buildings set against the beach. For the main shot, stand at the lookout, turn to face the beach and keep the curve of the sand running diagonally through the picture. Include a strip of palm foliage at one edge to add depth and frame the view.
text.geographic_location: Kamala Beach is on the west coast of Phuket, facing the Andaman Sea. The Laem Singh lookout sits on the headland between Kamala and Surin, about 860 m north-west of the beach.
text.directions_text: Head for the Kamala area, or Patong or Surin if you are staying there, and go by hired scooter or other road transport to the Laem Singh Viewpoint on the coastal road. The lookout is roadside, on the coastal road. If you are already at the north end of Kamala Beach, you can walk along the coastal road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the bay. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the headland or a single stretch of sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Laem Singh Viewpoint (roadside lookout on the headland between Kamala and Surin, looking back over Kamala). Kamala Beach curving below a palm-fringed headland, with the open Andaman Sea beyond. Face south-east, looking back over Kamala.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the sweep of the beach along one of the diagonal lines, with the sea in the lower or upper third. Let a few palm leaves intrude at one edge so the picture has a foreground. If you have time, Kamala Viewpoint offers a second look at the whole beach in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the water to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Panorama mode also works well here if you hold the phone steady and sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is the favourite for sunset shots here, but check where the sun is going and whether the trees will block it. Arrive early enough to try other spots along the coast if they do.

text.access_note: The Laem Singh lookout is a roadside stop with no entry fee; for Wat Baan Kamala, check the official site before you go and dress respectfully.
